subject: Physics
description: Magnetic poles, field, lines of force, Earth's field, electromagnets, ferromagnetism

questions.stem: If a bar magnet is broken into two pieces, each piece will:

options.option_text: Become a single isolated north or south pole
Behave as a complete magnet with both N and S poles
Lose its magnetism completely on breaking
Reverse the original direction of its magnetic field

questions.explanation: Magnetic monopoles have NEVER been observed. Every piece of a broken magnet becomes a smaller bar magnet with its own N and S poles. Repeating the cut yields more, smaller magnets — fundamental property of matter at the dipole level. Distractor 1 = monopole, hypothetical / unobserved. Distractor 3 — breaking does not destroy domain alignment in ferromagnets. Distractor 4 — direction does not flip.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Magnetic field lines, by convention, run:

options.option_text: From the south pole to the north pole outside the magnet
From north pole to south pole outside the magnet
Always in straight horizontal lines through the magnet
From the centre of the magnet outward to infinity

questions.explanation: Outside a magnet, field lines emerge from N pole and enter S pole; inside, they go S → N (forming closed loops). Lines never cross. Density of lines = strength of field. Distractor 1 reverses direction (a common confusion). Distractor 3 — lines curve, they don't go straight. Distractor 4 — lines form closed loops, do not go to infinity.

questions.stem: A freely-suspended magnetic needle aligns roughly along the north-south direction because:

options.option_text: Earth has its own magnetic field acting on the needle
Earth's gravity pulls the needle toward true geographic north
The needle's mass is greatest at one of its ends
Wind currents blow the needle into a fixed direction

questions.explanation: Earth behaves like a giant bar magnet (slightly tilted from its rotation axis). The magnetic needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field lines. The needle's geographic 'north' end (called the N-pole) actually points to Earth's MAGNETIC SOUTH POLE (which is near geographic north) — that's why opposite poles attract. Distractor 2 — gravity acts vertically downward, not horizontally toward north. Distractor 3 — mass distribution is irrelevant for orientation. Distractor 4 — wind has no role indoors.

questions.stem: An electromagnet is generally constructed by:

options.option_text: Permanently magnetising a hard steel cylinder
Winding insulated wire around a soft iron core
Heating a piece of iron near a permanent magnet
Cooling iron filings with liquid nitrogen at low temperature

questions.explanation: Electromagnet — current through a coil produces a magnetic field; placing a soft-iron core inside concentrates and amplifies the field by orders of magnitude. Removing current → field disappears (key advantage over permanent magnets — controllable). Used in electric bells, relays, MRI scanners, scrap-yard cranes, motors. SOFT iron is preferred over hard steel because soft iron loses magnetism quickly when current is off (low retentivity); steel retains residual magnetism, making the device less switchable.

questions.stem: Materials like iron, cobalt, and nickel that are STRONGLY ATTRACTED by magnets are classified as:

options.option_text: Diamagnetic — like copper, water and bismuth
Ferromagnetic — strongly attracted, can be magnetised
Paramagnetic — weakly attracted, like aluminium
Non-magnetic — completely unaffected by any field

questions.explanation: FERROMAGNETIC: iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium — domains align with external field; can be permanently magnetised; strong attraction. PARAMAGNETIC: aluminium, magnesium, oxygen, platinum — weak attraction; doesn't retain magnetism. DIAMAGNETIC: copper, water, gold, bismuth, silver — slight repulsion (induce opposing field). The Curie temperature is the point above which a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.

questions.stem: Earth's magnetic field protects us from harmful solar wind. The region of space carved out by this field is called the:

options.option_text: Stratosphere — a layer rich in ozone gas
Magnetosphere — extends thousands of km outward
Ionosphere — important for radio-wave reflection
Heliosphere — a region centred on the Sun itself

questions.explanation: MAGNETOSPHERE — Earth's magnetic field forms a teardrop-shaped cavity in the solar wind, deflecting charged particles. Charged particles trapped in this region form the Van Allen radiation belts. When solar particles do enter at the polar cusps, they cause AURORAE (Northern + Southern Lights). Distractor 1 = atmospheric layer with ozone. Distractor 3 = ionised upper atmosphere. Distractor 4 = the Sun's own magnetic-field bubble.

questions.stem: Above which temperature does a ferromagnet (e.g., iron) lose its ferromagnetism and behave only as a paramagnet?

options.option_text: The Boyle temperature, around 27 °C
The Curie temperature, ~770 °C for iron
The Boiling point of iron, around 2860 °C
The Critical temperature of liquefaction

questions.explanation: Curie temperature (after Pierre Curie). At this point, thermal agitation overcomes the alignment of magnetic domains; the material loses spontaneous magnetisation. Iron: 770 °C. Cobalt: 1115 °C (highest of pure elements). Nickel: 358 °C. Above Curie temp, ferromagnet → paramagnet. Used in some thermal switches, electrical cookers (rice cookers detect end-of-cooking when bottom heats past Curie point of a sensor magnet). Distractor 1 — Boyle temp is a gas-law concept. Distractor 3 — boiling point is much higher and unrelated. Distractor 4 — Critical temp is for fluid liquefaction, different physics.
